claims.text: The ability to form a protective, adherent oxide layer governs the coating's overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
Increasing Cr or another oxide-forming element relative to the baseline composition will promote formation of a nanostructured oxide layer.
The modified coating will form a continuous, nanocrystalline surface oxide during high-temperature sliding.
The oxide film will form more readily and adhere better in the modified alloy than in the baseline coating.
The enhanced oxide layer will increase surface hardness.
The enhanced oxide layer will reduce defect nucleation.
Increased hardness and reduced defect nucleation will limit microscopic plastic flow and localized deformation during sliding.
Limiting local plastic deformation through the oxide barrier will reduce wear.
Above approximately 500°C, the Cr-enhanced coating will have a lower wear rate than the baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Above approximately 500°C, the Cr-enhanced coating will exhibit less microscopic deformation than the baseline coating.
The reduced microscopic deformation may include diminished grain-boundary sliding or surface softening.
The baseline coating forms a less continuous or weaker oxide layer than the modified coating during high-temperature sliding.
Oxidation kinetics become significant in the stated operating regime above approximately 500°C.
At lower temperatures or under non-oxidative conditions, the protective-oxide mechanism may not dominate wear resistance.
